Cohort Analysis: the depth treatment

1. Two tables, two opposite errors

On 6 October 2026, Sudeshna Kamat, Chief Product Officer of Karghaa Systems in Pune, was handed a single slide by her board's audit chair. Karghaa sells warehouse-execution software to third-party logistics operators; the slide showed month-six retention by go-live quarter falling in a straight line — 79 per cent for accounts that went live in the last quarter of 2024, then 77, 71, 66 and 61. The audit chair's inference was blunt and, on the face of the numbers, reasonable: the product was deteriorating, and the ₹31 crore of mid-market pipeline the 2027 plan rested on should be paused until it stopped. Sudeshna had eleven days before the plan went to the full board.

On 9 November 2026, Faraz Qureshi, co-founder and head of product at Takli Studio in Bengaluru, walked into a board meeting with the opposite slide. Takli sells a ₹1,499-a-month assistant that turns a designer's sketch into a manufacturable tech pack, and its month-one retention by signup month had gone 62, 62, 62, 76 and 74 per cent from April to August. Faraz wanted to take quarterly paid acquisition from ₹40 lakh to ₹1.6 crore on the strength of it, arguing that a fourteen-point jump meant the product had finally landed and that no capital Takli could deploy would be cheaper than capital spent acquiring users who now stayed.

Both readings are wrong, in mirror-image ways. Karghaa's decline was largely not the product; Takli's improvement was largely not the cohorts. Both errors come from one place: a cohort table contains three effects that arithmetic cannot separate, so every conclusion drawn from one is an unstated assumption about which of the three to hold still. Saying that assumption out loud is most of what expertise consists of here.

2. The idea, and the traditions that disagree about it

A cohort is a set of units entering a system in the same interval of time, and cohort analysis tracks each set along its own clock — age, or time since entry — rather than the calendar. The output is a triangular table: cohorts as rows, age as columns, calendar time along the diagonals.

Its oldest parent is the actuarial life table — Halley's 1693 Breslau mortality work and the cohort life tables after it — built to answer what a cross-sectional death rate cannot: is this generation living longer, or is the population merely younger? Demography supplied the formal statement of the difficulty, in Norman Ryder's 1965 paper on the cohort as a concept in the study of social change. Consumer lending reached the same instrument independently as vintage analysis, tracking loss curves by origination quarter, because a portfolio's blended default rate says nothing about whether this quarter's underwriting is worse than last quarter's. Software borrowed it in the 2000s, and by the time the analytics vendors shipped cohort tables as a default view, a method carrying three centuries of caution about confounding had been re-imported as a dashboard widget with none of it.

Four schools now disagree about what such a table licenses.

The identification school, from demography and epidemiology, holds that age, period and cohort effects are perfectly collinear and so not jointly estimable from the table alone. It signs that the table is descriptive and that any causal reading needs a restriction supplied from outside the data. It will not sign the standard product move — reading down a column and calling the difference cohort quality — because that silently assumes no period effects.

The operator school — the growth-analytics lineage most product managers learned from — treats the table as a management instrument, not an estimator. It signs that a table recomputed weekly catches large, real regressions faster and cheaper than any experiment. It will not sign spending six weeks on a mix-adjusted decomposition before telling the team something broke.

The causal-inference school holds that only randomisation identifies a product effect, and that a cohort comparison is at best a quasi-experiment with an unusually strong confound, since anything that changes the product on a date also changes who arrives on it. It signs a difference-in-differences against a control cohort. It will not sign a launch declared successful because next month's cohort looked better.

The heterogeneity school, from the Pareto/NBD and beta-geometric work of Schmittlein, Morrison and Colombo and later Fader and Hardie, insists a cohort is a mixture of user types with different constant hazards, and that the flattening of a retention curve is sorting rather than growing loyalty. It signs that two cohorts with identical twelve-month curves can have materially different tails, and will not sign a single retention number as a property of a cohort.

3. Mechanics in depth: the three effects and how to pull them apart

Write r(c, a) for the retention of cohort c at age a, observed in calendar period p. The binding constraint is definitional, not statistical:

p = c + a

Fit the saturated model r = μ + αa + βp + γc and it will not identify: any linear trend moves freely between the three terms without changing the fit. One table therefore supports "the product is getting worse", "we are acquiring worse users" and "last quarter was bad for everyone" with equal statistical comfort. Choosing among them is judgement dressed, in most reviews, as reading.

Experts do not solve the problem — it has no solution inside the table — but impose a restriction they can defend, then check that the data behaves as it predicts. Three do most of the work. No period effects is the unstated default. A reference set of identical cohorts asserts that some run of cohorts differed only by noise, fits an age curve to them, and treats later residuals as period. Mix standardisation reweights every cohort to a common composition and asks what survives.

Karghaa's table is the standardisation case. An account counts as retained at age a if it holds a paid contract that month and at least sixty per cent of its licensed seats closed a task in it — usage-qualified, because Karghaa's contracts are annual and logo retention would hide a problem until renewal.

The eighteen-point fall is real; the question is what it is made of. Karghaa sells to two quite different buyers: enterprise 3PLs running more than forty warehouses, and mid-market operators running fewer than ten. In 2024 Q4 the split was 74 per cent enterprise; by 2025 Q4, after the mid-market motion opened, 28 per cent. Segment-specific month-six retention was 84 per cent enterprise and 65 mid-market in 2024 Q4, and 82 and 53 in 2025 Q4, and both blended figures reproduce exactly: 0.74 × 84 + 0.26 × 65 = 79.1, and 0.28 × 82 + 0.72 × 53 = 61.1.

Direct standardisation asks what 2025 Q4 would have shown had its composition matched 2024 Q4's: holding the mix at 74/26 and using 2025 Q4's own within-segment rates gives 0.74 × 82 + 0.26 × 53 = 74.5 per cent. Of the 18.0-point decline, 13.4 points are composition and 4.6 are genuine within-segment deterioration.

The second-order finding mattered more. The residual is not diffuse degradation: enterprise barely moved, 84 to 82, while mid-market fell 65 to 53. Karghaa was not shipping a worse product; it was shipping the same product into a segment it was getting worse at serving. Mid-market accounts sold through Karghaa's channel partner received a three-day implementation package rather than the eleven-day package direct sales included, and the three-day accounts reached month six at 44 per cent against 69.

Two steps are usually left implicit. The first is checking the diagonals before believing anything about the columns. Read diagonally, Karghaa's table shows a synchronous two-to-three point dip across every living cohort in the October–December 2025 quarter, recovering in January — the configuration freeze 3PLs impose on their own IT during the festive peak. It is transient, so it does not explain the level shift, but a team that had not looked would have no way to know. The second is exposure: a quarterly cohort mixes accounts that went live on the first day with accounts that went live on the last, and at age one the latter have had a third of the observation window. Anchor each account's clock to its own go-live date and count age in completed days.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the cohorting event is observed cleanly and its definition has not changed across the history compared. Two: composition is stable across the rows compared, or has been measured and standardised. Three: no calendar-time event affects all living cohorts inside the window, or the diagonals have been inspected and any such event indexed out. Four: cohorts are large enough that the differences read exceed sampling error.

Karghaa passes one and fails two spectacularly, which is why standardisation rescued the analysis. It passes four only barely: at 38 accounts, the 2024 Q4 cohort's 79 per cent carries a standard error near 6.6 points, so adjacent-quarter comparisons are close to meaningless and only the five-quarter trend is legible. Takli passes two and four comfortably and fails three — the failure more data cannot fix.

Cohort analysis is actively misleading, not merely uninformative, in three situations. When acquisition spend is scaling, cohort quality and cohort size are mechanically anti-correlated, because incremental spend buys progressively worse-matched users; a company judging the product by its cohort table during a ramp will conclude the product is decaying when it is only reaching further. When value is episodic rather than habitual — tax filing, insurance renewal, board-exam preparation — the age axis measures distance from a seasonal peak rather than decay, and cohorts starting at different points in the season are not comparable at all. And when the product is non-stationary, changing underneath every living cohort at once, a cohort is no longer a group experiencing a fixed product at different ages. That case used to be rare; in AI-native products it is normal.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Takli Studio is the non-stationary case in its purest form. On 1 August 2026 it swapped its underlying model, and the share of tech packs accepted without manual correction rose from 54 to 71 per cent overnight, for everyone. Faraz's month-one column looks like five cohorts of which the last two are better. The row shape says otherwise.

The April cohort went 62, 49, 41 — exactly the reference curve — then rose to 44 at month four. A rising cohort curve is nearly always an artefact, because retention is a survivor function and survivors cannot be un-churned; the ordinary explanations are a period effect, a definition change, or resurrected users credited back to their origin cohort. Here it is the first, and the proof is that every living cohort jumped in the same calendar month at a different age: April at age four, May at three, June at two, July at one. Dividing each cell by the reference value at that age yields a residual of almost exactly 1.22 for every August cell and 1.19 for every September cell, regardless of cohort. One multiplicative period index absorbs the whole pattern, and divided out, the five cohorts are indistinguishable from each other and from the reference.

The other edge cases share the structure if not the drama. In a two-sided marketplace such as Tagaa Sutra, a Surat platform matching yarn mills to garment units, the table runs twice, once per side, and neither curve is informative alone: a buyer cohort's retention depends on the supply liquidity present in its own first eight weeks, so a cohort acquired during a drought is not comparable to one acquired after it however identical the buyers. Mature marketplaces cohort buyers on a liquidity band — matched sellers in their district at signup — rather than the calendar, converting an uncontrolled period effect into a measured covariate.

Regulated products hit a denominator problem. Charkha Health, a Chennai diagnostics and teleconsultation platform, operates under the consent-expiry and erasure rights of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act; users who withdraw consent leave the analytics store entirely. The oldest cohorts therefore shed members from the denominator as well as the numerator, biasing their apparent retention upward, since a user who deletes an account is exactly the sort who had already stopped using it. Charkha's answer is a frozen denominator snapshot taken at cohort close, held as an aggregate count that survives individual erasure.

Hardware-plus-software products have several clocks and no agreement on which is the cohort's. Rehat Mobility, a Coimbatore electric two-wheeler maker with a connected-services app, can cohort by manufacture date, dealer invoice, delivery or app registration; these differ by up to five months, and the choice decides whether an inventory build-up looks like a retention collapse. The organisational seam is universal: at Karghaa, finance's cohort — contract start, logo, quarterly — and product's — go-live, usage-qualified, monthly — differ by eight points for the same accounts in the same meeting, and neither is wrong. Mature companies publish both and forbid the two from sharing an axis.

6. Nine things an expert notices that a competent practitioner does not

The identifying restriction is never written down. Every conclusion depends on holding one of age, period and cohort fixed, and the restriction is chosen, not estimated. The tell: ask what would have to be true for the column read to be valid, and the answer comes back about data quality rather than calendar events. The obvious reading — that the table shows whether newer users are better — fails because it cannot distinguish a better cohort from a good month.

Cohort quality is endogenous to spend. Scaling acquisition buys users further from the product's natural fit, so the table degrades as a direct consequence of growth working. The tell is a decline starting in the same quarter as the acquisition ramp and worst in the largest cohorts. The object of study is retention within channel; the decision is about channel economics, not roadmap.

The denominator is a policy choice. Whatever defines cohort entry is a gate, and moving it moves the curve without moving any user's behaviour: harder activation shrinks cohorts and they retain better; frictionless signup swells them and they retain worse. The tell is cohort sizes moving proportionally more than rates. Nothing got worse; the population being measured changed.

Rising cells are almost always artefacts. Any cell where retention at age a exceeds age a−1 deserves a stop-the-meeting question; the causes are a period effect, a changed definition, or resurrected users credited to their origin cohort. The tell is a rise at different ages in different rows but the same calendar month. That users rediscover the product as they mature is almost never the answer.

The newest column is the least trustworthy and the most quoted. The freshest cell is partial — the month is not over, the pipeline has not settled, late events have not landed — and it is the cell everyone reads because it is newest. The tell is a last column that reverts toward the trend each time the report is rerun. Two of Karghaa's five 2025 quarterly reviews turned on a final cell that later moved more than three points.

Blended retention can improve while every cohort worsens. If older, better cohorts grow as a share of the surviving base, the aggregate rises even as each row falls — Simpson's paradox at cohort level. The tell is company retention improving in a quarter when acquisition slowed. The obvious reading, that a retention initiative worked, inverts the truth: retention improved because growth stopped.

The table measures retention of a definition, not of value. A binary active flag hides depth: Karghaa's logo and usage-qualified retention diverged by eight points precisely because accounts were renewing while shrinking seat counts. The tell is a flat curve alongside falling revenue per surviving account. Experts run three triangles where novices run one — logo, usage-qualified and rupee retention — and treat the gaps as the finding.

A flattening curve is sorting, not loyalty. If a cohort mixes users with different constant hazards, the high-hazard ones leave first and the survivors are progressively enriched in low-hazard ones; the curve bends without any individual becoming more loyal. The tell is implied period-over-period retention rising monotonically and never settling. The missed consequence: two cohorts with identical twelve-month curves can have different long-run tails, because the same average comes from different mixtures.

Exposure inside the cohort window is unequal. A monthly cohort mixes users with thirty days of age-zero and users with one. The tell is a month-zero figure that tracks how many business days fell in the window. The fix — per-user clocks in completed days — is unglamorous and changes conclusions more often than any modelling choice above.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The real differences are frequency, unit and stationarity. High-frequency consumer products support weekly cohorts because the behaviour recurs weekly; Takli, on a monthly cycle, is monthly. B2B and enterprise products change the unit from user to account, collapsing sample sizes — Karghaa's entire 2024 Q4 cohort is 38 accounts — and forcing the analyst to read trends across five quarters rather than differences between two. Enterprise adds a second complication: buying and usage decisions sit with different people, so account retention composites an annual renewal decision with a daily usage one, and the two need separate triangles. Marketplaces need two-sided, liquidity-banded cohorts. Hardware needs a defensible clock. AI-native products need the period index as a standing fixture, because the model changes more often than the cohorts do.

Stage changes the binding constraint, not the method. Early companies are sample-size constrained: a forty-person weekly cohort swings ten points on noise alone, and the honest response is to widen the window rather than narrate the wobble. Growth-stage companies are mix-constrained, because channel composition moves fastest then. Late-stage companies are seam-constrained: data is plentiful but definitions have drifted across three analytics migrations, so the expensive work is provenance. What does not differ, though it is sometimes claimed to: the arithmetic, the identification problem, and the obligation to read the diagonals.

8. Three worked examples

The first two are already on the table. Karghaa's decomposition turned an eighteen-point headline into a twelve-point mid-market implementation problem — roughly ₹6.4 crore of recurring revenue at risk across the 2026 cohorts — and did not support pausing the mid-market motion, because the segment's poor retention traced to an onboarding package Karghaa controlled and could price differently. Takli's period index turned a fourteen-point improvement into a level shift applying equally to users acquired four months earlier: good news about the model, no news about the marginal acquired user.

The third is a failure, and it failed at the layer above all the analysis. In February 2025, Rehat Mobility's connected-services team cohorted riders by app-registration month and found the February cohort reaching month six at 23 per cent against a trailing average of 58. The team concluded connected services had no durable appeal, and the ₹2.1 crore roadmap for remote diagnostics and battery-health subscriptions was cancelled in May.

The cause was mundane and invisible from inside the analysis. A dealer group onboarded that month had registered the app for customers on shared showroom handsets before handover; roughly four thousand five hundred February accounts were created by a device the rider never held. The curve was measuring dealership tablets. Recovery took two forms. The immediate one was re-anchoring the cohort to the first authenticated ride completed on a handset the owner had logged into, and re-running fourteen months of history under both definitions — the step teams skip, because re-running history is tedious and the new number is the one they wanted. The durable one was a provenance rule: any change to a cohort-defining event must be backfilled across trailing history and the two triangles diffed cell by cell before either is quoted. Catching it late cost nine months of roadmap, a subscription business restarted from scratch in 2026, and the product manager who had argued the number was wrong and could not prove it.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Comparing cohorts at different ages is the commonest failure and the most easily caught. The warning sign is a chart with calendar dates on the horizontal axis; the diagnostic question is "what age is each of these points?"; the cost of catching it late is embarrassment rather than money, because the error is obvious once named.

Definitional drift is the most expensive. The warning sign is a retention gap that widens or narrows with no product change to explain it, often in the month a team migrated analytics tools. The diagnostic question is "when did the event definition last change, and was history backfilled?" Rehat's ₹2.1 crore is typical of the late-catch cost: definitional failures destroy roadmaps rather than quarters, because they surface after the decision is implemented.

Mistaking a period effect for a cohort effect is the most consequential for capital allocation. The warning sign is a change appearing in several rows at once at different ages; the diagonal read is the diagnostic and takes an afternoon. Faraz's late-catch cost would have been ₹1.2 crore of incremental quarterly spend committed against a retention assumption the marginal user was never going to meet.

Averaging across a right-censored triangle is the quietest. The warning sign is a blended curve dipping sharply at exactly the ages only the newest cohorts have not reached, because blanks were read as zeros. The diagnostic question is "how many cohorts contribute to this cell?"; the cost is a systematically pessimistic long-horizon retention assumption feeding straight into lifetime-value models and acquisition budgets.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest live disagreement is whether the cohort table is an instrument or an estimator. The operator position, at its strongest: experiments on six-month retention are almost never adequately powered — Karghaa would need several hundred accounts per arm to detect five points, more than it signs in two years — and a fast, biased instrument read weekly beats an unbiased one that never arrives. Its evidence is the record of real regressions caught by cohort tables and nothing else. The causal position, at its strongest: the confound is structural, since whatever changes the product on a date also changes who arrives on it, so the comparison is biased in an unknown direction — Karghaa and Takli being the same error pointing opposite ways. For the operator position to be wrong, mix would have to move as fast as product quality, which in a scaling company it does. For the causal position to be wrong, the effects that matter would have to swamp the confound, which they sometimes do.

The second disagreement is about the primitive. One camp holds acquisition date to be the wrong cohorting variable — a proxy for whatever actually changed — and that cohorting on channel, use case or onboarding path explains three or four times the variance the calendar does. The opposing view is that this holds only for variables you thought of in advance, and that the calendar is universal precisely because it catches changes nobody anticipated. Most mature teams cohort by date for detection and by covariate for explanation.

The third is definitional and will not be settled, because it is a disagreement about whose question matters. Product argues that a paying account with no usage is churn not yet booked; finance argues that it is revenue, it is auditable, and usage-qualified retention is an unfalsifiable number whose threshold the product team can move. Both are correct; the only defensible practice is to keep both triangles and treat the divergence as a leading indicator in its own right.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this reads the diagonals before the columns, and asks what changed in calendar time before asking what changed about the users. They state the identifying restriction aloud, in one sentence, before presenting the conclusion. They know their cohort sizes well enough to say without computing that three points between two forty-account cohorts is nothing. They keep three triangles and treat the gaps as findings. They are suspicious of every rising cell. They can say precisely what the table cannot answer — Takli's has nothing whatever to say about what the next ₹1.6 crore of paid acquisition will buy — and they say it before being asked. And they treat the cohort definition as infrastructure under change control, not a dropdown in a dashboard.

12. What they decided

Sudeshna did not pause the mid-market motion. She took the decomposition to the board with the mix effect and the residual separated, argued that the evidence pointed at an implementation package rather than the product, and asked for the eleven-day package to be priced into every mid-market deal from January. She declined to claim causation — channel-sold accounts differ from direct-sold in more than package length — and funded randomised assignment of the longer package across the next sixty channel deals, accepting an answer in the third quarter of 2027.

Faraz staged the spend: ₹55 lakh rather than ₹1.6 crore, every rupee cohorted by channel with a fifteen per cent geographic holdback, and a plain statement to the board that Takli's retention had improved for reasons that said nothing about acquisition quality. He also made the period index standing, recomputed monthly against a rolling reference, on the argument that where the model changes quarterly, calendar effects are the default state of the data rather than an occasional nuisance.

Three questions for discussion. First: Sudeshna's standardisation assumed the two segments were themselves stable in composition — what would have to be true inside mid-market for the 4.6-point residual to be mix again, one level down? Second: if Takli's upgrade had lifted new cohorts more than old ones, as a genuinely better first-run experience might, how would Faraz separate that from the uniform period effect he found, and how much data would he need? Third: both protagonists recommended an experiment they will not read for three quarters — when is it right to act on the cohort table in the meantime, and on what evidence?

13. Going deeper

Defining activation (the aha moment) sets the gate every cohort passes through; move it and every curve here moves. Retention curves and the PMF signal is the next question once cohorts are clean: whether the curve plateaus or decays to zero is the sharpest read on fit a team will get. Segmenting users in analytics supplies the covariates standardisation needs. Cohort-level P&L and payback curves attaches money to the triangle, where Faraz's decision actually lived. Segment migration and lifecycle segments handles what cohort analysis cannot: users who change type mid-life. Constructing a funnel and reading drop-off explain why a cohort is the size it is before it begins ageing, and stickiness and natural frequency fixes what age interval is meaningful. Feature adoption analysis is this table applied to a launch, with the same period confound and less awareness of it. Root cause analysis of a metric change turns a cohort finding into a cause, and signal vs noise keeps a forty-account cohort from generating a quarter of strategy. Product vs measurement is the standing question behind the whole argument: did the number move because the product changed, or because the instrument did?

Cohort Analysis

Ritika Anand, VP of Product at Chaubara, a Gurugram-based payments app for delivery and ride-hailing partners, spent the second Tuesday of April 2026 rereading the same slide before her quarterly review. Chaubara's signature feature, Bachat Box, skims a slice of every partner's daily payout into a locked savings pot; partners can turn it off, but for the first three years of the product's life they had to turn it on. On 15 February, Ritika's team flipped that default: Bachat Box now started switched on, and a new partner had to actively opt out. Sign-ups since then looked healthier on every early chart the growth team produced. The question on the table was not whether the redesign moved a metric — it plainly had — but whether the partners it was moving were the same kind Chaubara had always kept, or a more fragile kind that would look good for six weeks and vanish by month three. The CFO wanted an answer before authorising a ₹4.2 crore rollout of the same default-on logic to Chaubara's new lending product, where a wrong guess would be expensive twice over: provisioning for loans to partners who would not stick around to repay them, or losing the head start of shipping to lending immediately if the early signal was real. Ritika could not answer the question by looking at how many partners were active that week, because that number blended January's design with March's and said nothing about whether the March partners behaved differently as they aged. What she needed was to isolate people by when they started and watch each such group age on its own clock. That method is cohort analysis, and it is the reason this page exists.

The idea

A cohort is simply a group of users who share a starting point in time — typically the week or month they signed up, made their first purchase, or were first exposed to a product. Cohort analysis is the practice of tracking each such group separately over the weeks or months since it started, rather than looking at the whole user base as one undifferentiated pool on a single calendar timeline. The problem it was invented to solve predates software by decades: actuaries and epidemiologists needed to compare the life expectancy of people born in different years without being fooled by a population's average age shifting as older members die off and younger ones are born; consumer lenders later adapted the same logic into "vintage analysis," tracking the default rate of loans originated in each quarter separately, because a portfolio's blended default rate says nothing about whether this quarter's loans are riskier than last quarter's. Web and mobile teams borrowed the technique in the 2000s as usage data became cheap to collect, and analytics platforms such as Mixpanel and Amplitude built cohort tables into their core dashboards soon after, which is largely why the term now sounds native to software even though its lineage runs through banking and public health. The sentence Ritika could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a raw trend line tells you what happened to your product; a cohort table tells you whether newer users are healthier or sicker than the users who came before them.

How it actually works

Building a cohort table starts with a decision practitioners often make so quickly they forget they made it: choosing the event that defines when a user "starts." Chaubara's team used the date a partner registered a bank account for payouts, not the date they downloaded the app, because plenty of partners installed the app days before they trusted it enough to link a bank account, and counting from install would have buried real behaviour under registration friction that had nothing to do with Bachat Box. The second decision, equally load-bearing, is choosing the behaviour being tracked over time — the "return" event. Ritika's team defined a partner as active in a given week if they completed at least one Bachat Box transaction that week, not merely if they opened the app, because the CFO's question was specifically about savings behaviour, not general engagement.

With those two definitions fixed, the mechanics are arithmetic rather than mystery. Every partner is assigned to a cohort by the week their bank account was linked. Time is then measured not in calendar weeks but in weeks-since-start for each cohort, so that a January cohort's "week 4" and a March cohort's "week 4" are directly comparable even though they fall on different calendar dates. For each cohort, the analyst counts how many of its original members were active in week 0, week 1, week 2, and so on, and expresses each count as a percentage of the cohort's starting size. Laid out with cohorts as rows and weeks-since-start as columns, the result is the classic cohort table, or "cohort triangle" — triangular because a cohort that started eight weeks ago simply does not yet have a week-twelve figure to report, a fact that is easy to state and surprisingly easy to forget when reading the table quickly, as the figure below shows.

Fig. 1 — Each row ages on its own clock; the triangle's blank corner is not missing data, it is time that has not passed yet.

Reading the table by column, not by row, is the discipline that makes cohort analysis useful rather than merely tidy. Reading down the week-4 column, Ritika could compare 39% (January), 46% (February) and 55% (March) on equal footing, because each figure describes a cohort at the same age, four weeks old, regardless of which calendar month that fell in. That column is where her answer would live.

A worked example

Chaubara's January cohort — partners who linked a bank account between 1 and 31 January — numbered 8,400. Of those, 3,276 completed at least one Bachat Box transaction in their fourth week, which the table reports as 3,276 ÷ 8,400 = 0.39, or 39%. The March cohort numbered 9,150, larger partly because a concurrent marketing push widened the top of the funnel; of those, 5,033 were active in their own week 4, giving 5,033 ÷ 9,150 = 0.55, or 55%. On the single dimension the CFO cared about, the March cohort was retaining savings behaviour sixteen percentage points better than January at the same age, and the sixty-five points at week 2 versus January's fifty-one told the same story earlier and more sharply. That gap, replicated across three successive weekly cohorts after the 15 February change, was Ritika's central piece of evidence that the opt-out default was not merely inflating a vanity number but changing durable behaviour.

The second pass is where a careless analyst gets burned. Ritika's data lead reran the same table with one input changed: "active" redefined from "completed a Bachat Box transaction" to "opened the app," a far looser bar. Under that definition, January's week-4 figure rose from 39% to 71%, and March's rose from 55% to 76% — the gap between the two cohorts nearly disappeared, falling from sixteen points to five. Nothing about the partners had changed between the two passes; only the yardstick had. The looser definition was picking up partners who opened the app to check their payout balance out of habit, whether or not the redesign had changed their saving behaviour at all, which diluted exactly the signal Ritika needed to isolate. The lesson generalises well beyond Chaubara: a cohort curve is only as meaningful as the activity it counts, and changing that one input can move the story from "the redesign worked" to "we cannot tell" without a single new partner joining the app.

The nuances a learner must catch

Cohort by acquisition date is not the only useful cut

Time-of-signup is the default cohorting variable because it is always available, but it is a proxy for whatever actually changed on that date — a redesign, a pricing change, an acquisition shift. Where a team can name the real driver, cohorting by it directly, such as "referred by an existing partner" versus "acquired through paid ads," often explains more variance than the calendar date does, and Ritika's team re-cut March by channel to confirm the gain was not just warmer leads.

A cohort curve describes a group, not a person

A 55% week-4 retention rate does not mean each March partner is 55% likely to be active in a given week; it means 55% of the original 9,150 were active that specific week, and who is included can shift week to week. Two cohorts can post identical aggregate curves while one retains the same core users every week and the other churns and re-acquires different users each week — a distinction the table alone cannot show without a look at individual repeat-activity patterns.

Cohort size interacts with the confidence you should place in the curve

A cohort of 9,150 supports a 55% estimate with reasonably tight uncertainty; a cohort of ninety does not, and a start-up team reading week-by-week swings in a forty-person weekly cohort as meaningful signal is usually reading noise. The remedy is either to widen the cohorting window from weekly to monthly, trading resolution for stability, or to wait for more data before drawing conclusions.

Right-censoring, not missing data

The blank week-12 cell for the March cohort in Figure 1 is not an error or a gap to be filled; the cohort is six weeks old at the time of reporting and week 12 has not occurred yet. Analysts new to the technique sometimes average across a triangle as though the blanks were zeros, which silently and badly understates recent cohorts' true retention.

Cohort analysis is routinely confused with segmentation

Segmentation slices a user base by a static trait — geography, plan tier, device — measured at a point in time; cohorting slices by a moment in time and then tracks the group's behaviour as it ages. The two are complementary and frequently combined, as when Ritika's team later asked whether the March retention gain held equally for partners in tier-two cities versus metros, but they answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

Survivorship bias hides inside every cohort curve

By definition, a cohort's week-12 figure describes only the partners who were still around long enough to be measured at week 12; it says nothing directly about the far larger number who dropped out earlier, and it is tempting to study the survivors' habits and mistake them for the cause of survival rather than a consequence of it.

A cohort table shows correlation with a launch date, not proof of causation

The March cohort retained better than January's, and the redesign shipped on 15 February — but a marketing push, a competitor's app crashing that same month, or a change in payout timing could each independently move the same number. Cohort analysis is a diagnostic that narrows the search for a cause; on its own, without a controlled experiment or at least a clean pre/post comparison with other explanations ruled out, it does not close the case.

Cohort analysis cannot tell you why, only whether and by how much

Even a clean, well-defined, adequately sized cohort table answers "did retention change and by how much," never "why partners behaved differently." Ritika still needed qualitative interviews with a sample of March partners to learn that many of them experienced the default-on pot as a form of forced discipline they had wanted but never enabled themselves — a mechanism the curve alone could not reveal.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and stage

The shape of a useful cohort table changes with the kind of product it describes. In a high-frequency consumer app like Chaubara's, weekly cohorts are natural because the underlying behaviour — a daily payout, a daily ride — happens often enough to measure on that clock. A B2B product with a monthly billing cycle and few weekly active seats per account, such as workflow software sold by a company like Sadan Cloud to mid-sized logistics firms, produces noisy weekly cohorts; the sensible unit there is the account, cohorted by contract start month and tracked on a monthly or quarterly clock instead. In a two-sided marketplace such as Haveli Stay, a homestay booking platform, cohort analysis has to run twice, once for guests and once for hosts, because the two populations churn for different reasons and one blended curve would average away both stories. Stage matters too: an early team with a few hundred users per cohort should expect noisy curves and resist over-reading a single week's wobble, while a company at Chaubara's scale can treat small, consistent gaps between cohorts as real signal worth acting on.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is comparing cohorts at different ages as though comparable — reading "January is at 30% now" against "March is at 55% now" without noticing one cohort is twelve weeks old and the other four. The symptom is a chart plotted against calendar date rather than weeks-since-start; the fix is to always plot weeks-since-start on the x-axis, never the calendar.

The second is changing the definition of "active" partway through a comparison, exactly as the app-open re-cut above illustrated, often because a dashboard's default metric quietly changed when the team switched analytics tools. The symptom is a retention gap that mysteriously narrows or widens with no product change to explain it; the diagnostic is to check the event definition before hunting for a product explanation.

The third is treating a cohort table as proof of causation rather than a lead. The symptom is a team shipping a change and declaring victory the moment the next cohort's curve looks better, without checking whether anything else shifted at the same time; the cheapest diagnostic is to look for a second, independent line of evidence — an A/B test, a clean pre/post with no confound, or at minimum a check on whether acquisition mix changed alongside the product change.

The fourth is averaging a triangle across incomplete rows, treating blank right-censored cells as zero. The symptom is a blended retention curve that dips sharply and mysteriously at exactly the ages only the newest cohorts have not yet reached; the fix is to compute averages only across cohorts old enough to have a real value at that age.

What good looks like

By the third week of April, Ritika's team had a week-4 column showing 39%, 46%, and 55% across three successive cohorts since the redesign, each cohort large enough to trust, each measured against the same activation definition, cross-checked against an acquisition-channel cut that ruled out warmer leads as the sole explanation, and supported by partner interviews explaining the mechanism. That combination — a clean cohort table, a ruled-out confound, and a plausible causal story — is what separates a defensible recommendation from a chart that merely looks encouraging.

Closing

Ritika recommended the CFO fund the ₹4.2 crore lending rollout, but with the default-on logic applied only after a partner had completed eight weeks of stable Bachat Box activity, since her cohort evidence spoke to savings behaviour, not repayment behaviour, and she was careful in the room to say so rather than overstate what the table could prove. The natural next topic for anyone who has followed this argument is retention curves and the PMF signal: once cohorts are built correctly, the shape of the curve itself — does it flatten into a plateau or decay toward zero — becomes the sharper question, because a plateau is often the clearest quantitative signal of product-market fit a team will ever see. Two questions worth sitting with: if Chaubara's March cohort had been half the size, at what point would Ritika have been wrong to trust the 55% figure at all; and what other change, besides the redesign, might independently explain why March's partners looked healthier than January's?

Vrishti Finserv: The Grid That Would Not Agree

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 7 December 2025. Six exhibits, four of which contradict each other, an exclusivity contract that expires in seven weeks, and a board offsite in eleven hours.

1. Sunday night

Kavya Ramaswamy had printed the exhibits because she thought better on paper, and by nine in the evening the dining table of her flat in Koramangala held six sheets arranged in an order she had changed four times. Outside, the December air had the particular dryness that follows Bengaluru's late monsoon. Her laptop showed an unanswered message from Ipsita Deb in Toronto, timestamped 10:41 a.m. Eastern: "I can rebuild 2024 onward on either definition. I cannot rebuild 2023 on any of them. Please don't put 2023 on a slide."

The board offsite began at eight the next morning at Vrishti Finserv's office off Bannerghatta Road. Two items sat on the agenda under Kavya's name. The first was a recommendation on whether to serve notice on the Vaahak Logistics distribution agreement before the 31 January deadline, after which it renewed automatically for four years. The second was a single line that Devdutt Bhattacharya, Vrishti's co-founder and chief executive, had added himself on Friday evening: "Cohort quality — CPO to present a view."

Kavya had a view. She had, in fact, four of them, and each one was supported by a different exhibit on the table in front of her.

2. How Vrishti got here

Vrishti Finserv was founded in Bengaluru in 2020 by Devdutt Bhattacharya and Anjali Kaul to solve a problem that India's gig economy had created and not solved: delivery riders, cab drivers and warehouse hands earned daily but were paid weekly or fortnightly, and the gap was filled by informal lenders at rates nobody wrote down. Vrishti's first product was an instant payout — a rider could settle the day's earnings to a bank account or UPI handle the same evening for a flat ₹9. It was small, honest and enormously sticky in its first year.

Three products followed. Vrishti Save let a worker route a fixed slice of each payout into a partner bank deposit. Vrishti Advance offered ₹2,000 to ₹15,000 against earned wages, underwritten by Hemadri Capital, an NBFC, with Vrishti acting as a lending service provider under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions. Vrishti Plus, launched in February 2025 at ₹49 a month, bundled unlimited free payouts, a small accident cover and fuel cashback. By November 2025 Vrishti had 62 lakh registered users, 18 lakh monthly transacting users, and ₹287 crore of revenue in the year to March 2025.

One decision from 2023 shaped everything afterwards. In October of that year, with growth flattening at around 60,000 new users a month, Devdutt signed a four-year exclusive distribution agreement with Vaahak Logistics, a last-mile aggregator that supplied delivery capacity to quick-commerce and e-commerce platforms across twenty-two cities. Vaahak made Vrishti the default payout partner for its nine lakh registered delivery partners. Vrishti paid a 22 per cent share of revenue earned from those users and agreed not to sign comparable agreements with Vaahak's two largest competitors for the life of the contract. Signups went from 60,000 a month to 1.2 lakh a month within a quarter, and by 2025 roughly three-quarters of everyone joining Vrishti arrived through a Vaahak fleet.

The agreement also did something less visible. It made Vrishti's user base a function of one partner's recruitment pipeline. When Vaahak onboarded 40,000 riders in a month for a festival surge, Vrishti acquired 40,000 users whose relationship with gig work was six days old.

3. The industry around it

India's gig workforce had, by most estimates, crossed 1.2 crore people, spread across the delivery fleets of Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto, Blinkit, Flipkart and Amazon, the cab networks of Ola and Uber, and thousands of smaller logistics operators. The policy scaffolding was arriving quickly: the Code on Social Security's gig-worker provisions, the e-Shram registry, and state-level legislation in Rajasthan and Karnataka creating welfare funds financed by platform levies. Every one of these raised the prospect that platforms themselves would offer the financial services Vrishti sold.

Competition came from three directions at once. PhonePe and Paytm reached the same users with UPI and could bundle payouts at near-zero marginal cost. Razorpay and similar players sold payout rails to the platforms directly, which meant a platform could disintermediate Vrishti by buying the pipe. And the platforms themselves — several of which had built rider-facing wallets — could simply stop needing an intermediary.

Regulation shaped the credit business precisely. Under the RBI's digital lending framework, Vrishti as an LSP had to surface a Key Fact Statement, route all money flows directly between the borrower and Hemadri Capital, and honour a cooling-off period during which a borrower could exit without penalty. A revision effective April 2025 tightened disclosure and lengthened the cooling-off window. The DPDP Act added a further constraint that nobody had anticipated in analytical terms: when a user withdrew consent, Vrishti deleted their event history, which meant historical cohort denominators shrank retroactively. Roughly 1.4 lakh users had withdrawn consent during 2025.

Vrishti's global exposure was real but small. Grace Wong in Singapore ran a remittance pilot for Indian gig workers employed by logistics firms in Dubai and Sharjah, with 11,000 users. Sandeep Rao, VP Enterprise Partnerships in New Jersey, was six months into selling a white-labelled Vrishti to two American logistics groups with large Indian delivery operations, a deal worth a reported ₹34 crore a year if it closed.

4. The situation in detail

The story Vrishti told itself changed three times.

Through 2024, the belief was that Vaahak users were better users. Ipsita's first cohort grid, presented in September 2024, showed the H1 2024 cohort — the first substantially Vaahak cohort — retaining at 68 per cent at one month against 64 per cent for H1 2023. Devdutt used the slide in the Series C deck. What was not examined at the time was that Vaahak riders received a ₹200 joining credit funded by Vrishti, redeemable only through a payout, which mechanically produced a first-month transaction for anyone who opened the app at all.

In November 2024, the definition of an activated user changed. Farhan Siddiqui's growth team, working against an activation target, moved the bar from "two instant payouts in the first thirty days" to "one instant payout or a savings pot opened". Activation jumped from 45 per cent to 63 per cent in a month. The old definition was dual-run for exactly one month and retired on 1 December 2024. Every retention figure computed on activated users from that date forward has a different denominator from every figure before it.

Through 2025, the belief was that the base was maturing. Then, on 14 November 2025, Lakshmi Narayanan Iyer — Lux to everyone — circulated Hemadri Capital's quarterly credit pack. Hemadri's vintage curves for Vrishti Advance showed 90-day delinquency at six months rising from 2.2 per cent for the Q3 2024 disbursal vintage to 3.8 per cent for Q2 2025. Lux's covering note said, in one line, that Vrishti was acquiring worse borrowers.

Two days later Ipsita produced Exhibit 1, which appeared to agree with Lux, and Farhan produced Exhibit 2, which appeared to contradict both. What nobody had reconciled by the evening of 7 December was that Hemadri's vintages were grouped by month of disbursal and Vrishti's cohorts by month of signup — so a single Hemadri vintage contained borrowers drawn from eighteen different Vrishti cohorts, and a single Vrishti cohort's members appeared in up to six Hemadri vintages.

5. The people

Kavya Ramaswamy, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Position: the company does not currently know whether its users have got worse, and should say so. Incentive: her credibility with the board rests on the product organisation not having caused the decline. Not saying: she approved the July redesign of the payout flow herself, over Marius's objection, and has not tested whether it affected the July and August cohorts.

Devdutt Bhattacharya, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: renew Vaahak, on improved terms, and stop litigating the past. Incentive: a Series D conversation is open with two funds, and Vaahak's volume is the growth story. Not saying: he has already told Vaahak's founder, informally, that Vrishti would go to a 25 per cent revenue share to secure a longer term.

Farhan Siddiqui, Head of Growth, Gurugram. Position: engagement is improving and the transacting-user metric is too narrow; Exhibit 2 is the truer picture. Incentive: his team's targets are activated users and monthly actives, both of which look excellent. Not saying: the activation redefinition went in without written sign-off from finance or product, and he knows the balance-notification deep link his team shipped in March 2025 generates app sessions counted as activity.

Ipsita Deb, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: nothing should go to the board until the grids are rebuilt on one definition of activation and one definition of retention. Incentive: professional accuracy, and a strong dislike of being quoted selectively. Not saying: she cannot reproduce any 2023 figure at all, because the June 2025 pipeline migration left pre-2024 events only as monthly aggregates, and she is embarrassed that she did not raise this before the migration.

Lakshmi Narayanan Iyer, Head of Credit Partnerships, Mumbai. Position: cut Advance disbursals to Vaahak-sourced users by half until the vintages stabilise. Incentive: he owns the relationship with Hemadri and a delinquency spike is his problem first. Not saying: Hemadri has privately indicated it may reduce approval rates by 30 days' notice regardless of what Vrishti decides, which would make the decision moot.

Marius Lindqvist, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the July payout-flow redesign degraded the experience for low-literacy users and the July onward cohorts show it. Incentive: he opposed the redesign's scope and would like that on the record. Not saying: he also wants the same redesign credited with the 31 per cent Plus attach rate, which cannot be true of both.

Grace Wong, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: the Gulf corridor cohorts retain at nearly double the Indian rate and deserve investment. Incentive: her remit grows if the corridor is funded. Not saying: the corridor has 11,000 users in total and her retention figure rests on a single cohort of 900.

Ajinkya Kulkarni, Engineering Manager, Pune. Position: the analytics migration is complete and sound; the historical gap is a known, accepted trade-off. Incentive: the migration was his project and it shipped on time. Not saying: consent-withdrawal deletions under the DPDP Act are being applied to the historical event store, so cohort sizes from 2024 are quietly smaller each month than they were when first reported.

Sandeep Rao, VP Enterprise Partnerships, New Jersey. Position: none on cohorts; he wants a clean retention story to put in front of two American logistics buyers by January. Incentive: his ₹34 crore deal. Not saying: one of the two buyers has asked for cohort data by employment tenure, which Vrishti does not collect.

7. Voices

"We are comparing a 2023 user who found us on their own with a 2025 user who was handed a phone with our app already on it and told to use it for payouts. Of course the curves differ. The question is whether that is a problem or the whole point of the Vaahak deal."

Farhan Siddiqui, email to the leadership group, 18 November 2025

"I can give you the number you want. I can give you four different numbers you want. What I cannot give you is one number that is true across the whole period, because we have changed the activation definition once, the return event twice, and the event pipeline once, and we deleted part of the history in between. Please stop asking me which cohorts are better until we agree what a cohort is."

Ipsita Deb, Slack thread #metrics-review, 21 November 2025, 01:14 IST

"Hemadri will not wait for our analysis. They have their own committee and their own board, and their committee looks at Exhibit 3 without any of the context we are debating here. If 90-plus goes past four per cent on the Q3 vintage they will cut approvals, and then the question of whether we should cut disbursals will have answered itself."

Lux Iyer, credit partnership call, 2 December 2025

"The July redesign removed the confirmation screen. For a rider who reads slowly, in their third language, that screen was the only place the ₹9 fee was visible before the money moved. I said so in June. I would like the record to show the July cohort's numbers."

"Both American buyers have asked the same question and neither has asked it the way we measure. They want retention by how long the person has been doing delivery work — not by how long they have had our app. We do not have that field. Could we get it before January?"

Sandeep Rao, note to Kavya, 28 November 2025

8. The options as Kavya sees them

Option one: buy a quarter. Tell the board that the company cannot presently answer the question, commission a full restatement of every grid on a single set of definitions, and defer the Vaahak recommendation to the January board call — seventeen days before the notice deadline. The upside is honesty and a defensible number in February. The cost is that Devdutt loses the Series D narrative for a quarter, Hemadri acts on its own timetable regardless, and the restatement cannot recover 2023 at all, so the comparison that started the argument will remain unavailable even after the work is done.

Option two: renew Vaahak and treat the decline as the price of scale. Accept that a channel delivering users at ₹38 will produce lower retention than one delivering them at ₹22, argue that ₹96 of contribution on 74 per cent of signups is a better business than ₹770 on 15 per cent, and recommend renewal at the improved revenue share Devdutt has already hinted at. The upside is volume, simplicity and a growth story. The cost is four more years of exclusivity, a base whose composition Vrishti does not control, and a diligence process in which a sophisticated investor rebuilds Exhibit 1 unaided.

Option three: serve notice and diversify. Give notice by 31 January, negotiate a shorter non-exclusive arrangement, and redirect the acquisition effort towards the platform partners and the direct channel that Exhibit 4 says are worth three to eight times as much per user. The upside is a better base and freedom to sign the competitors currently excluded. The cost is that Vrishti loses perhaps 70 per cent of its signup volume within two quarters, that the direct channel has never been scaled deliberately, and that Sandeep's American buyers are buying reach as much as retention.

Kavya had written all three on a sheet, and beneath them, in smaller handwriting, a fourth line she had not shown anyone: all three of these assume the problem is which users we acquire. Sandeep's note had lodged uncomfortably. Vrishti measured a user's age from the day they joined Vrishti. The Vaahak riders who arrived in 2024 and 2025 were, disproportionately, people in their first months of gig work — a population that leaves gig work itself at a rate Vrishti had never measured and did not collect the data to measure. If the cohorts were decaying because the workers were exiting the industry rather than the app, then acquisition channel was the wrong axis, the product had not failed, and neither renewing nor cancelling the Vaahak contract addressed anything at all.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board offsite began at eight on Monday, 8 December. Notice on the Vaahak agreement had to be served in writing by 31 January 2026 or the contract renewed for four years on existing terms. Vrishti held ₹390 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹18 crore a month, a runway of roughly twenty-one months, and had been under a headcount freeze since October, which meant any restatement would be done by Ipsita and one analyst in Bengaluru. Hemadri Capital could reduce approval rates on thirty days' notice at its sole discretion, and under the RBI's framework Vrishti could neither guarantee the loans nor direct Hemadri's credit policy. The DPDP Act obliged Vrishti to continue honouring consent withdrawals, which would continue to alter historical cohort sizes. Sandeep's enterprise contracts required a retention disclosure by 31 January. And the Series D term sheets, if they came, would come in February.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibits 1 and 2 are computed from the same cohorts and support opposite conclusions. What exactly differs between them, and what would you need to see in order to decide which is measuring something Vrishti should care about?

2. Exhibit 3 groups users by a different clock from every other exhibit. What can and cannot be inferred by placing it beside Exhibit 1, and what would a correctly aligned version of Exhibit 3 look like?

3. Identify three separate events on Illustration 1 that would show up as changes in a cohort grid without any user having behaved differently. For each, say which direction of the grid — row, column or diagonal — would reveal it.

4. Exhibit 4 shows Vaahak users with the lowest transacting retention and the highest Plus attach rate, during a period when fleet supervisors were paid ₹35 per Plus activation. What are the plausible explanations, and what single piece of evidence would most cheaply distinguish between them?

5. Kavya's unwritten fourth line proposes that the cohort axis itself is wrong — that the relevant clock is tenure in gig work, not tenure on Vrishti. If she is right, which of the three options remains sensible, and what would Vrishti have to build, measure or negotiate in order to find out? If she is wrong, what has she cost the company by raising it on the morning of a board offsite?

6. It is Monday morning. What does Kavya do, in what order, and what does she say to the board about the Vaahak renewal — given that she cannot, by 31 January, have a restated set of numbers she trusts?

11. Eleven hours

At a quarter past eleven Kavya moved Exhibit 6 to the top of the pile, then moved it back. The seasonality point was the cleanest thing she had: every H2 cohort in the company's history had its third month in January, and nobody had ever adjusted for it, which meant some unknown part of the fall from 44 to 36 in Exhibit 5 belonged to the Indian delivery calendar rather than to anything Vrishti had done. It was also the least useful thing she had, because it explained a portion of a decline without telling her whether the remainder was product, channel, definition or the industry itself.

Ipsita's message was still unanswered. Devdutt had sent one at half past ten — "Keep it simple tomorrow. The board wants direction, not epistemology." — and Kavya had typed three replies and sent none of them. On the table, six exhibits said six things. The instant-payout business that Vrishti had been founded on was, on the only definition that had been stable since 2022, shrinking inside every cohort that had joined since the Vaahak deal. The engagement business Farhan described was growing inside those same cohorts. The credit business was deteriorating on a clock nobody had aligned. And the contract that had produced all of it renewed itself in fifty-four days unless somebody wrote a letter.

She turned off the lamp at ten past midnight without deciding anything, and lay awake working out what she would say if the lead director asked the only question that really mattered — not whether the newer users were worse, but how long Vrishti had been in a position to know.

Chaska: Are the New Subscribers Worse?

Hyderabad, November 2025. A subscription cooking app has trebled its monthly sign-ups and halved its retention. The chief executive wants a redesign rolled back. The head of product has five days to decide whether he is right.

1. The decision

At half past eight on the evening of Sunday, 23 November 2025, Aditi Raghavan was still at the Chaska office in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with the lights off in the rest of the floor. On Friday the 28th she had to present a Q4 growth plan to the board, and the plan had to say what Chaska would do with ₹6 crore of remaining budget before Sankranti and Pongal in mid-January — the busiest cooking fortnight in Chaska's year, when downloads in Telugu, Tamil and Kannada roughly doubled.

The plan also had to answer a question that Vikram Shenoy, Chaska's co-founder and chief executive, had put to her on Thursday in one sentence: "Roll back Voice Mode, then we talk about the budget." Vikram believed the September redesign of the cooking flow had damaged the product. The evidence he cited was that the monthly churn rate on Chaska Plus had risen from 7.9 per cent in February to 13.4 per cent in October, while sign-ups had never been higher. Aditi was not sure the two facts were connected at all, and she had until Friday to say so with numbers.

2. Chaska

Chaska was founded in 2019 by Vikram Shenoy and Meenakshi Rao around a simple observation: India's most-watched cooking content was in regional languages and almost none of it was designed to be used while actually cooking, with wet hands, in a small kitchen. Chaska commissioned home cooks across Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh to record short recipes in their own languages, then wrapped each recipe in a step-by-step cooking mode with timers, portion scaling and an ingredient list that could be handed off to Swiggy Instamart, Zepto, Blinkit or BigBasket in two taps.

By October 2025 the free app had 3.1 crore installs. Revenue came from two places. Chaska Plus, at ₹149 a month or ₹1,199 a year, removed advertising and unlocked saved meal plans, offline recipes and the hands-free cooking mode; it was collected through UPI Autopay mandates under the Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework, with cards as a fallback. Affiliate commissions on grocery handoffs made up the rest. Annualised revenue stood at ₹71 crore, of which about 62 per cent was subscription. The company was six weeks from opening a Series C round, and the deck's headline was a promise to cross one lakh net Plus subscribers by the end of the March quarter.

Chaska's competition was everything and nothing: no direct rival at scale, but YouTube cooking channels, Instagram Reels, and the recipe content that Swiggy and Zomato published for free. Its defensible position was the cooking mode itself and the regional-language creator network, and both of those were product, which is why Vikram's instinct ran to a product explanation.

3. The situation

The decline was not in dispute. Chaska Plus had added 11,200 paying subscribers in February and 29,300 in September — very nearly a trebling — and the net base had moved from 58,000 to only 84,000, well short of the pace needed for the one-lakh promise. Blended monthly churn had risen almost every month since April.

Three explanations were live in the company. Vikram's was Voice Mode. Farida Qureshi, who ran growth marketing from Mumbai, said the app was fine and the base was simply younger, since a younger base always churns more. Rohit Menon, Chaska's data scientist in Toronto, had said in a Slack thread at two in the morning Indian time that both of them were arguing about an average and neither had looked at the cohorts, and had then spent a weekend building Exhibit 1.

A fourth voice complicated matters. Shreya Pillai, who led customer success from Singapore and covered the large Gulf diaspora base, had filed 340 support tickets in late July from users in Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi whose subscriptions had lapsed without warning. Chaska's engineering team in Pune had traced it to the company's own scheduler, which had stopped sending the pre-debit notifications that RBI's e-mandate rules require before an autopay debit; without the notification, the mandate could not be presented, and around 4,100 subscriptions across every tenure had silently lapsed between 14 and 26 July. Engineering had fixed the scheduler on the 27th. Nobody had thought to ask what it did to the retention numbers, because it had been logged as a payments incident rather than a product one.

4. The people

Aditi Raghavan, Head of Product, Hyderabad. Two years at Chaska, previously at a Bengaluru edtech firm. She owns the roadmap and will own the consequence of rolling back a redesign her team spent a quarter building. She wants an answer she can defend in front of a board, not an argument she can win in front of a chief executive.

Vikram Shenoy, co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad. He wrote the first version of the cooking mode himself. He wants the Series C closed at a good price, which means he wants the one-lakh number, and he believes product quality is the only durable moat Chaska has. He is instinctively suspicious of growth-marketing explanations because they always seem to conclude that nothing is the product's fault.

Farida Qureshi, Head of Growth Marketing, Mumbai. She is measured on cost per paying subscriber, which has fallen from ₹640 to ₹310 since April. The fall is almost entirely due to the bundle deal she negotiated with Tejas Mobiles, a fast-growing Indian handset brand that preloads Chaska on its sub-₹12,000 devices and offers a first month of Plus at ₹49, sharing 30 per cent of subsequent revenue. She wants the ₹6 crore put behind the bundle and a second preload deal before Sankranti.

Rohit Menon, Data Scientist, Toronto. He has no stake in the outcome and a strong preference for being right. He believes the blended churn number should never have been in a board pack and says so more often than is politic across a 10.5-hour time difference.

Exhibit 3 unsettles both of the confident positions in the company. Farida's bundle, the channel with the worst retention by a wide margin, returns ₹145 per subscriber against a cost of ₹95 — thin, but positive, and it scales. Performance marketing, which nobody had questioned, returns ₹50 per subscriber and is the weakest use of a rupee that Chaska has. Creator referral is worth five times the bundle and fourteen times performance marketing per subscriber acquired, and it is the only channel Chaska does not currently fund with a dedicated budget.

6. The options

Option A — roll back Voice Mode and pause acquisition spend. This is Vikram's instruction. Its upside is that it restores the chief executive's confidence and costs no money. Its cost is a quarter of engineering time, a demoralised design team in Berlin, and — on the evidence of Exhibits 1 and 2 — the repair of something that was never broken, while the actual mix problem continues unaddressed through Sankranti.

Option B — put the ₹6 crore behind the bundle and sign a second preload deal. This is Farida's plan. It is the only option that reliably delivers one lakh net subscribers by March, because the bundle is cheap and its volume is predictable. Its cost is that Chaska's base becomes majority-bundle, its blended retention continues to fall, and it enters a Series C diligence process in which an experienced investor will build Exhibit 1 themselves and ask why the cohort curves are collapsing.

Option C — re-plan spend on cohort contribution, cap the bundle, and fix what the diagonal revealed. Move the majority of the ₹6 crore from performance marketing to the regional creator-referral programme; hold the bundle at its current run rate rather than expanding it; make good the July mandate failure by offering the 4,100 lapsed users a restored subscription; and replace blended churn in the board pack with the cohort grid. Its upside is the highest contribution per rupee and an honest set of numbers going into diligence. Its cost is that creator referral scales slowly and unpredictably, and that the one-lakh promise almost certainly slips a quarter.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, what can be concluded about Voice Mode, and what cannot? Which direction of reading the grid supports each conclusion?

2. What exactly does the shaded diagonal in Exhibit 1 show, and why would it be invisible in a blended monthly churn figure?

3. Farida's cost per paying subscriber has fallen by half and Chaska's retention has fallen with it. Is she succeeding at her job? What should she be measured on instead, and who would have to agree to the change?

4. What should Aditi recommend on Friday, and how should she present the one-lakh promise to the board?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about the difference between an average and a comparison. Chaska's blended churn rate is an average over subscribers of every tenure, and in a company whose sign-ups have trebled in eight months, the tenure mix is moving far faster than anybody's behaviour. Cohort analysis fixes that by grouping subscribers by the month they started paying and comparing groups only at equal age — which is what makes the question "are newer subscribers worse?" answerable at all.

A well-reasoned answer reads Exhibit 1 in three directions and says what each one means. Across a row is a single cohort ageing, and February's row shows a perfectly respectable curve. Down a column is the like-for-like comparison, and it does show real deterioration in the blended cohort. Down a diagonal is a calendar month hitting every tenure at once, and the shaded cells locate the July mandate failure precisely. The answer then decomposes the column: Exhibit 2 shows every channel's own retention constant, which means the column moved because the weights moved, not because the product changed. Finally it notices the timing: Voice Mode shipped in September and the decline starts in April, so the redesign cannot be the cause. A learner who stops at "newer cohorts are worse, therefore the product is worse" has read one direction out of three.

One defensible path is Option C, with a modification. Aditi should present Exhibits 1 and 2 to Vikram before Friday, privately, and secure the decision not to roll back — the redesign is exonerated by dates alone, and she should say so without triumph. She should then argue for reallocating the ₹6 crore on contribution rather than on cost per subscriber, which moves money out of performance marketing first, because Exhibit 3 shows it returning ₹50 per subscriber against creator referral's ₹744. She should hold the Tejas bundle at its current level rather than cutting it, because ₹145 of contribution is real money and the channel reaches households Chaska's creator network does not, but she should insist that the bundle's subscribers be reported separately from here on, so that one number never again hides two businesses. She should restore the 4,100 lapsed subscriptions, which is cheap, right, and worth roughly ₹49 lakh of annualised revenue. And she should tell the board that one lakh net subscribers is achievable by March only through the bundle, that reaching it that way would lower the quality of the base an investor will inspect, and that she recommends against it — offering instead a cohort-contribution target that the company can defend in diligence.

The path is defensible rather than certain. It trades a visible milestone for an invisible one, it depends on a creator-referral programme that has never been scaled, and it asks a founder to abandon a product explanation he believes in six weeks before a fundraise. The point of the cohort grid is not that it removes the judgement; it is that it tells Aditi which of the three arguments in her company is about something real.
